comments.author: @MattBellzminion
comments.text:
I grew up in Pinecrest, back when it was part of unincorporated Dade County [itself since renamed, to "Miami-Dade County"]. My family home was roughly 2000 square feet, on a little over a quarter acre, with a 32-foot-long (~ 10m) pool. That's all well and good, but to maintain the yard, driveway edges, and clipped bushes and hedges, we had to devote several hours a week to yardwork during the wetter part of the year, downshifting to every other week or even every third week (but that was pushing it) the rest of the year. The pool also had to be maintained and vacuumed regularly. Need I remind everyone that doing several hours' worth of yardwork in Miami is no joke, when the temperatures and humidity were in the 80s-90s, with plenty of mosquitoes to add to one's discomfort? By the time I was a teenager, I was feeling what I would later learn is called "alienation" from this upper-middle-class lifestyle and felt somewhat envious of the residents of a few townhouse developments several miles from my suburb. 

As for the roads and sidewalk infrastructure, I lived on the cusp of a short stretch of residential blocks with a sidewalk facing the main N-S avenue and leading to my elementary school, but that investment in safety and aesthetics for little kids walking to school (my brother and I being two of them) only extended for three blocks north of the school. There was no general neighborhood network of sidewalks, but my parents didn't express any worries re. our safety because the local streets were so wide and straight, they could easily accommodate their two lanes. Unfortunately, their capaciousness also encouraged motorists to speed, and I often felt anxious biking along the avenues in areas where I had to share the road with cars. We kids out walking (but mostly biking) probably would've been safer with a Dutch-style blueprint of narrower streets and a network of sidewalks and bike paths, but building and maintaining those would've cost something. 

So it goes. This was after all an UNINCORPORATED suburb well south of the metro core of Miami and its proximate towns (Hialeah, Coral Gables, South Miami, etc.), and a big part of the appeal of this Ur-Pinecrest area was its relatively low property taxes, which made it popular with younger couples raising kids in what they hoped was a perfectly safe area, in a conservative, mostly deeply Southern state with no state income tax ('cuz the higher-taxes-and-social-benefits tradeoff is for socialists and commies, don'tcha know).

In a place with very low corruption, you get what you pay for; with more corruption, you get notably less, but that subject warrants its own conversation...
